newsitem.title: UK: Euro crude outlook - Chill lines sellers' pockets.
newsitem.headline: Euro crude outlook - Chill lines sellers' pockets.

text.p: Some of the coldest temperatures seen in Europe for several decades and the possibility of weather-related disruption to Russian exports should ensure a bright start to 1997 for sellers of European spot crude oil.

Strong demand for heating oil, boosted by householders feeling the chill of a colder than normal winter which shows no sign of ending soon, will encourage refinery buyers returning from holiday to pick up marginal barrels, traders said.
"They may have left their offices for Christmas thinking they were covered but if this weather continues they'll want more," said a trader.
Private U.S. forecaster Weather Services Corp said on Friday temperatures in Europe would remain well below normal for the time of year over the next six to 10 days.

North Sea traders said differentials for remaining January cargoes would hold firm or even move slightly higher this week, largely as a result of strong local demand. "They could go higher -- we're in a potentially very strong period if the European demand holds up," said a North Sea producer.
"A lot of cargoes moved last week at higher prices in private trade," said a trader.
The value of benchmark Dated Brent, which began the year as it ended 1996 at the mercy of opposing factions looking to influence related swaps trade, was set to rise, he said.
A cargo due to load Jan 17-19 was offered at Feb Brent +25 cents on Friday, four cents higher than the previous deal.

Unconfirmed talk of underproduction on the Brent field -- last week Shell UK cancelled a cargo due to load Jan 15-17 in response to a request "from the Brent field system coordination unit" -- and an open arbitrage to the US also helped sentiment.

The premium for Louisiana Light Sweet over Dated Brent stood at a healthy $1.50 a barrel on Friday, off its recent highs but still workable despite a surprise build in U.S. crude stocks in the week to December 27, they said.
"The arb to the States is still open but we don't need that much more to move out of the region," said one.
Sour crude markets in the Mediterranean would draw support from seasonal weather-related disruption at Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk and a reduction in Iraqi export volumes.
Russia's leading export terminal was shut on Friday due to high winds and Med refiners were anticipating more of the same.
"January and February are the worst months for the Black Sea so we will have to wait and see how much of the (export) programme they will achieve," said one.
"Sour differentials should hold around current levels unless there is a prolonged cold spell," she added.
Iraqi exports in January from the Turkish outlet at Ceyhan should total about 260,000 bpd of Kirkuk blend, some 75,000 less than it sold in the second half of December, trading sources said.
